source.title: Downsampling leads to Image Memorization in Convolutional Autoencoders
source.authors: Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan; Mikhail Belkin; C. Uhler

page_placements.theme: Generative-model memorization differs from classifier fitting

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies memorization in autoencoders, including convolutional autoencoders, and shows that initialization and sufficient depth/downsampling matter. Its evidence refines the broad claim: these are reconstruction models trained on images, and some memorization results require near-zero initialization or particular architectures.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test the cited classification claim about fitting randomly assigned labels, training time under label corruption, or generalization on true labels. Rows below cover results on memorization in autoencoders only where they bear on the claim's stated versions. Statements about related prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures autoencoder reconstruction, projection onto training-data spans, and attraction to training examples. These are different outcomes from fitting random labels or learning real labels before noise. Gaussian inputs are used as reconstruction training data or test probes, without the classification task required by V3. References to the original studies supply context; the study neither tests nor operationally uses their random-label findings.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that overparameterized autoencoders learn maps concentrated around training examples: shallow fully connected models map into their nonlinear span, deep models exhibit local attraction, and sufficiently deep convolutional models show similar behavior. They also report that this memorization can coexist with low reconstruction error and persist under early stopping. Extension to classification is an expectation, not a demonstrated result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies autoencoder reconstruction and attraction to training examples, not classification with random labels. Its models, objective, and outcome measure differ from the original sources' random-label classification experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Memorization depends on architecture depth, width, downsampling, and initialization; large initialization can make memorization noisy, and shallow convolutional architectures can fail to memorize.

fits_no_version.finding: Fully connected and nonlinear convolutional autoencoders can recover training examples by iterating their reconstruction maps; greater width and depth increase recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterized autoencoders can learn reconstruction maps that contract toward training examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Shallow linear convolutional architectures can fail to learn projection-style memorization, while sufficiently deep or downsampling architectures exhibit it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection-style memorization in convolutional autoencoders depends on architecture and depth.

fits_no_version.finding: An MNIST autoencoder achieves train MSE 0.00117 and test MSE 0.00159 while iterated test trajectories converge to training examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attraction toward training examples can coexist with low test reconstruction error.

fits_no_version.finding: Kaiming-initialized networks show noisier recovery of training examples than the smaller-output initialization schemes examined.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Autoencoder reconstruction-map memorization can depend on initialization scale.

record.problems: The experiments are largely qualitative trajectory or image demonstrations. Some nonlinear convolutional memorization evidence is based on visual inspection because no nonlinear spectrum is available. Several experiments use very small training sets; initialization and architecture vary across examples. The study does not test random-label classification or report uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results on the claim's random-label classification versions were found. The paper also includes theorem statements and qualitative claims about early stopping or initialization that are not separate empirical outcomes beyond the reported rows.

untested.parts: Random-label classification training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Zero classification training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise training inputs using the same networks.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening classification test error across label-corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-label patterns before memorizing noisy labels; the study cites this finding without testing it.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6; this does not deny the reported autoencoder effects. The paper defines memorization through projection or attraction, which differs from fitting arbitrary labels. Its architecture and initialization dependencies therefore do not limit or challenge these claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train standard deep classifiers on completely random labels or report their training/test classification error.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels, or convergence versus corruption fraction.
No test of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs as training inputs to the stated classification task.
No sweep over randomly corrupted classification labels or corresponding test error.
No test of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their effect on fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
No training-time comparison of learning real-label patterns versus memorizing noisy or random labels; this behavior is mentioned only as cited prior work.

rows.subject: Fully-connected autoencoder (10 layers, 512 hidden neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Trained to convergence on 100 samples from the 3D Swiss Roll dataset; then iterated the learned map on 1000 uniformly spaced initial points.
rows.measure: Whether iterated trajectories converge to training examples
rows.value: Most of the trajectories converge to training examples.
rows.note: Autoencoder reconstruction memorization, not classification with random labels.
rows.check: Trajectory convergence measures autoencoder attraction, not any claim version.

rows.subject: Fully connected autoencoder (7 layers, 128 hidden neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Trained to convergence on 100 MNIST samples; iterated on random test examples.
rows.measure: Whether trajectories converge to training examples
rows.value: Trajectories converge almost exclusively to the training examples.
rows.note: The study describes a qualitative trajectory result.
rows.check: Recovery of training images through iteration does not measure random-label fitting.

rows.subject: Fully connected autoencoder (14 layers, 128 hidden neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Trained to convergence on 20 MNIST samples; tested by mapping arbitrary input images.
rows.measure: Whether arbitrary inputs map directly to training examples
rows.value: The training examples are superattractors; arbitrary input images map directly to a training example.
rows.note: Qualitative result for autoencoder reconstruction, not random-label classification.
rows.check: Mapping arbitrary images to training examples measures attraction, not random-label classification.

rows.subject: MNIST autoencoders of varying width and depth
rows.operation_detail: Varied autoencoder width and depth and measured recovery probability over iteration count.
rows.measure: Recovery probability of training examples as a function of iterations
rows.value: Increasing width and depth both increase the recovery rate.
rows.note: No exact recovery-probability values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Recovery versus inference iterations does not measure training convergence under label corruption. Split width and depth conditions if retaining these off-claim results.

rows.subject: Convolutional autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained to convergence on 100 CIFAR images; iterated on random test examples.
rows.measure: Whether trajectories converge to training examples
rows.value: Iterating the map yields individual training examples.
rows.note: The main text identifies CIFAR; the figure caption says CIFAR dataset.
rows.check: The result measures reconstruction-map attraction. The main text explicitly identifies the dataset as CIFAR10, although the caption says CIFAR.

rows.subject: Convolutional autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained on 10 CIFAR10 images, one from each class; mapped arbitrary inputs.
rows.measure: Whether arbitrary inputs map to training examples after one iteration
rows.value: After just 1 iteration, individual training examples are output.
rows.note: The text identifies the setup as nonlinear and uses leaky ReLU activations.
rows.check: One-step recovery of training images does not measure any claim version.

rows.subject: Linear convolutional autoencoders
rows.operation_detail: Trained on one image using gradient descent on mean squared error.
rows.note: The authors explicitly say this shallow linear convolutional autoencoder does not memorize arbitrary inputs.
rows.check: This is a theoretical rank result about projection-style memorization, not failure to fit training targets. It cannot establish absence of random-label fitting.

rows.subject: Linear convolutional autoencoders
rows.size_stated: 2 layers; filters of kernel size 3; any number of filters
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed memorization capacity for images of size 4 × 4 or larger.
rows.measure: Whether the architecture can memorize images
rows.value: Cannot memorize images of size 4 × 4 or larger.
rows.note: Specific negative result for an autoencoder architecture.
rows.check: The corollary concerns an architecture's inability to implement the paper's projection-style memorization; it does not establish inability to interpolate training data or fit random labels.

rows.subject: Linear convolutional autoencoders
rows.size_stated: 1, 5, or 8 layers; 1, 16, or 128 filters per layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on two normally distributed images of size 3 × 3; measured the learned solution spectrum.
rows.measure: Spectrum of learned solution as an indicator of memorization
rows.baseline: Memorization would have two eigenvalues equal to 1 and remaining eigenvalues close to 0.
rows.value: No examples memorize; spectra by layer/filter conditions: 1 layer—1, 1, .98, . . .; 5 layers—1, 1, .78, . . ., 1, 1, .72, . . ., 1, 1, .7, . . .; 8 layers—1, 1, .14, . . ., 1, 1, .1, . . ., 1, 1, .08, . . .
rows.note: Each spectrum is separately listed in the table under the layer/filter settings; the text says none of the examples memorizes and increasing filters has minimal effect.
rows.check: The spectrum measures projection-style memorization, not V3 input fitting. Table 1 uses 2, 5, and 8 layers, not 1, 5, and 8. The two-layer spectra are 1, 1, .98; 1, 1, .99; and 1, 1, .99 for 1, 16, and 128 filters. Split the nine layer/filter conditions.

rows.subject: Linear convolutional autoencoders
rows.size_stated: depths 3, 9, 29, 70, 144, 267, 10, 200, or 350; one filter per layer
rows.operation_detail: Trained with gradient descent to loss below 10⁻⁶; some deep networks used Adam and skip connections.

conditions.value: each parameter as close to zero as possible

rows.measure: Spectrum of learned solution as an indicator of memorization
rows.baseline: Memorization indicated by eigenvalue(s) equal to 1 and remaining eigenvalues with magnitude less than approximately 10⁻².
rows.value: Table 2 reports spectra: 2×2, 1 example, 3 layers: 1, [< 10⁻²]; 3×3, 1 example, 9 layers: 1, [< 10⁻²]; 4×4, 1 example, 29 layers: 1, [< 10⁻³]; 5×5, 1 example, 70 layers: 1, [< 10⁻⁵]; 6×6, 1 example, 144 layers: 1, [< 2 · 10⁻²]; 7×7, 1 example, 267 layers: 1, [< 4 · 10⁻³]; 3×3, 3 examples, 10 layers: 1, .98, .98, [< 10⁻²]; 5×5, 5 examples, 200 layers: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, [< 10⁻³]; 7×7, 5 examples, 350 layers: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, [< 10⁻²]
rows.note: Table 2 is an aggregate of nine distinct settings retained as a single row because the paper supplies spectra by condition; exact row splitting is constrained by the requested per-condition format and the table's compact, flattened layout. Training used Adam at learning rate 10⁻⁴ when depth exceeded 10; for networks over 100 layers, skip connections every 10 layers. The stated gradient-descent learning rate was 10⁻¹.
rows.check: Small reconstruction loss and low-rank spectra do not test classification on unstructured inputs. Split the nine Table 2 settings; their depths, image sizes, sample counts, optimizers, and skip connections differ.

rows.subject: Downsampling convolutional autoencoder D1
rows.operation_detail: Trained on two CIFAR10 images for 10000 iterations; evaluated its output on standard Gaussian data.

conditions.value: progressively downsamples to a 1 × 1 representation using stride 2

rows.measure: Rank/spectrum and output on Gaussian inputs
rows.value: Learned solution has spectrum 1, 1, [< 2 · 10⁻²]; Gaussian data outputs a linear combination of training images.
rows.note: Default PyTorch initialization was described as sufficient to keep each parameter close to zero.
rows.check: Gaussian data are test probes after training on CIFAR10 images, not Gaussian training inputs for V3.

rows.subject: Downsampling convolutional autoencoder D2
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a single CIFAR10 image for 10000 iterations; evaluated its output on standard Gaussian data.

conditions.value: downsamples 32 × 32 image to a 4 × 4 representation after layer 1; 29 layers

rows.measure: Rank/spectrum and output on Gaussian inputs
rows.value: Learned solution has spectrum 1, [< 7 · 10⁻⁶]; Gaussian data outputs a multiple of the training image.
rows.note: The paper describes this as memorization.
rows.check: Gaussian test probes reveal projection onto a training image; they do not measure fitting Gaussian training inputs.

rows.subject: Nonlinear convolutional autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a 4 × 4 image and evaluated using Gaussian-noise test inputs.
rows.measure: Whether the network recovers/memorizes the training image from Gaussian test inputs
rows.value: The network memorizes the 4 × 4 image, based on visual inspection.
rows.note: The authors say a nonlinear equivalent of the spectrum is unavailable, so this is visual evidence.
rows.check: Visual recovery from Gaussian test inputs measures attraction. The training image is a structured white-square image.

rows.subject: Nonlinear convolutional autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained on two orthogonal 2 × 2 images; evaluated on Gaussian test inputs.
rows.measure: Whether test inputs map to individual training examples or combinations
rows.value: Given new test examples, the network outputs individual training examples instead of combinations.
rows.check: Gaussian test inputs mapping to structured training images do not test V3.

rows.subject: Fully-connected autoencoder (7 layers, 512 hidden neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Trained to convergence on 50000 MNIST samples and evaluated test-set reconstruction and trajectories.
rows.measure: Train/test reconstruction MSE and convergence of test-image trajectories to training examples
rows.value: train MSE = 0.00117, test MSE = 0.00159; trajectories of test examples converge to training examples.
rows.note: The authors use this to show contraction can coexist with near-zero reconstruction error.
rows.check: Reconstruction MSE and attraction on clean MNIST do not measure classification generalization, random-label fitting, or explicit regularization. Separate reconstruction error from trajectory recovery if retaining these results.

source_check.locator_found: Supplementary Material I.1, Figure 11 caption, page 24

rows.subject: Nonlinear convolutional autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Compared behavior after initialization under Xavier uniform/normal and Kaiming uniform/normal strategies.

conditions.value: nonlinear version of Figure 3a autoencoder, with leaky ReLU activations

rows.measure: Output norm on training example before training and memorization quality on arbitrary inputs
rows.value: Kaiming uniform/normal output norms: 9.67 and 17.64; arbitrary-input outputs show noisy memorization.
rows.note: The text says Kaiming initialization does not present memorization as clearly as other initialization schemes; the exact mapping of each norm to uniform versus normal is given only in the figure.
rows.check: Initialization sensitivity concerns reconstruction-map memorization, not a claim version. Pretraining output norms are initialization diagnostics, not memorization outcomes; separate them from post-training qualitative recovery. The supplied text does not explicitly map individual norms to uniform versus normal initialization.
